docs.title: Siemens S7-1500 Production Cell + OEE Dashboard
docs.text:
A three-station simulated assembly cell run by an S7-1500, programmed with SICAR-style S7-GRAPH step sequences, operated from a WinCC HMI and connected over OPC UA to a live OEE dashboard.

Factory I/O · PLCSIM Advanced · TIA Portal · OPC UA · Python / Streamlit

S7-1500S7-GRAPHSCLWinCCOPC UAFactory I/OStreamlitSQLite

Cell design Dashboard View source files

docs.title: Why this project
docs.text: Production cells in automotive and assembly plants are programmed in a very particular way: step sequences with explicit interlocks and step supervision (the SICAR style), clear operating modes, an HMI that tells the operator why something is blocked, and production data flowing up to MES for OEE. I worked with Allen-Bradley and Siemens PLCs in industry; this project builds a complete Siemens cell end to end, in the open, from the I/O list to the OEE numbers.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Factory I/O scene  <── PLCSIM Advanced driver ──>  S7-1500 (PLCSIM Advanced)
                                                     ├─ FB_ModeManager
                                                     ├─ GR_Station1..3  (S7-GRAPH)
                                                     ├─ FB_Production  -> DB_Production
                                                     │
                                       WinCC HMI ◄───┤  (Profinet / HMI connection)
                                                     │
                                                     └─ OPC UA server
                                                            │
                                     python/dashboard/collector.py  -> SQLite
                                                            │
                                     python/dashboard/app.py (Streamlit): OEE, Pareto, MTBF/MTTR

Until the PLC exists, python/cellsim/server.py stands in for it: it runs the same three sequences, publishes the same OPC UA node ids under the Siemens namespace URI, and accepts the same HMI commands. Switching the dashboard to the real PLC is a URL change.

Until the PLC project exists, a mock S7-1500 OPC UA server stands in for it: it runs the same three sequences, publishes the same node ids under the Siemens namespace URI and accepts the same HMI commands. Switching the dashboard to the real PLC is a URL change.

docs.title: Demo script (planned video, 3–4 min)
docs.text:
1. Cell overview on the HMI, Auto, Start. Parts flow; the dashboard OEE rises.
  2. Force S1_PusherFront off in Factory I/O. GRAPH supervision trips fault 103 after 2 s; HMI alarm and station screen show the blocked step; stack light red.
  3. Stop, switch to Manual. Show a jog blocked by its interlock, with the reason on screen.
  4. Release the force, Reset, Auto, Start. The dashboard shows the downtime in the Pareto and the MTTR.

docs.title: Research paper ideas
docs.text: The production cell alone is a portfolio piece. Combined with the robot-joint actuator testbed (FOC on STM32, CAN/EtherCAT, Python logging) there are three realistic papers. Ranked by strength.

docs.title: 1. Actuator health data in the production cell's OEE loop (uses both projects)
docs.text:
Question. Can health indicators from a robot-joint actuator (phase current residuals, winding temperature, tracking error growth) predict a fault early enough that scheduling maintenance raises cell availability, compared with run-to-failure?

Method. The FOC testbed publishes health indicators over OPC UA (or CAN to a gateway). The cell's PLC or the Python side treats the actuator as a station resource. Inject degradations on the testbed (added friction, encoder noise, phase resistance change), feed the measured indicator traces into the simulated cell (cellsim already models faults, MTTR and OEE), and compare availability under run-to-failure, fixed-interval and condition-based maintenance.

Why it is timely. Humanoid robots built from exactly these actuators are moving into factory cells, and the integration of actuator-level health into line-level OEE is barely written about.

Venues. IEEE CASE, IEEE ETFA, IFAC conferences (check 2027 deadlines).

docs.title: 2. Current-signature fault detection on a robot-joint actuator
docs.text:
Question. How early and how reliably can a model-based residual (from the motor model already used for FOC tuning) detect common actuator faults, compared with a small learned detector, under realistic load profiles?

Method. Use the Simulink/Python motor model from the actuator project's first half to generate residuals; validate on hardware with injected faults. Report detection delay vs false-alarm rate (ROC), and compute cost on the STM32.

Venues. ACC, IEEE/ASME AIM, IECON. This is the natural seed of a master's thesis.

docs.title: 3. Data-driven supervision limits for PLC step sequences
docs.text:
Question. S7-GRAPH supervision times are usually set by hand (e.g. "2 s"). Can logged step durations set them statistically, trading false alarms against detection delay, and how much downtime does that save?

Method. Log step times per GRAPH step (from the cell over OPC UA, or from cellsim), fit a per-step distribution, set the limit at a target false-alarm rate, and compare detection delay and spurious stops with hand-set limits under injected jams. The simulator in this repo can already produce the data; the real cell gives validation.

Venues. IEEE ETFA work-in-progress track, INDIN, or a workshop. Small and fast, a good first paper from the Siemens project alone.

docs.title: Honest scope note
docs.text: Simulation-only results usually land as conference or work-in-progress papers. Ideas 1 and 2 with hardware data from the actuator testbed are journal-capable. Idea 1 needs the testbed working by about February to be realistic for a mid-2027 submission.

docs.title: Cell design and I/O list
docs.text:
Three stations on one conveyor line with a reject lane, built as a custom Factory I/O scene.

 Emitter ─► [S1 Infeed + vision] ─► transfer ─► [S2 Pick & place assembly] ─► [S3 Outfeed + count] ─► Remover
                    │                                    ▲ lids from a second emitter
                    └─► reject pusher ─► reject lane
Station Job Key parts in Factory I/O 1 Infeed and inspection Detect part, read type with the vision sensor, push wrong parts to the reject lane Emitter (bases, mixed with wrong parts), roller conveyor, diffuse sensors, vision sensor, pusher 2 Pick and place assembly Clamp the base at a stop, pick a lid, place it on the base, release Stop blade, clamp, 2-axis pick and place, lid emitter on a feeder conveyor 3 Outfeed and count Count good parts, remove them Roller conveyor, diffuse sensors, remover

Station 2 is the bottleneck (about 6.7 s nominal per part). The ideal cycle used for OEE is 6.0 s.

docs.title: Building the scene
docs.text:
1. Start a new empty scene. Use the stock Assembler and Sorting by Height scenes only as references for how the pick and place and pusher are wired.
  2. Place parts in the order of the table above. Name every sensor and actuator in Factory I/O exactly as the tag below; it makes the driver mapping one-to-one.
  3. Set the base emitter to mix in about 5 % of a different part (e.g. blue vs green raw material) so the vision step has something to reject.
  4. Drivers: choose Siemens S7-PLCSIM Advanced, select the instance, and map the tags to the addresses below.
  5. Demo fault: in Factory I/O you can force a sensor (right-click > Force). Forcing S1_PusherFront FALSE jams the pusher and trips supervision 103 after 2 s.

Save the scene as factoryio/production_cell.factoryio.

docs.title: WinCC HMI specification
docs.text: Target: WinCC Unified PC runtime (or a Comfort panel such as TP1200 Comfort if Unified is not in the license), simulated alongside PLCSIM Advanced.

docs.title: Rules for every screen
docs.text:
• One colour rule: grey idle, green running, yellow waiting / manual, red fault. Colour is never the only signal; every state also has a text label.
  • A fixed header on all screens: cell state, mode, active alarm count, date/time. Navigation buttons along the bottom.
  • Commands are pulses written to DB_HMI (Cmd_Start, Cmd_Stop, Cmd_Reset); the PLC resets them. The HMI never writes process outputs directly.

docs.title: Screens
docs.text: # Screen Content Tags 1 Cell overview Line mimic: three stations, conveyors and reject lane, each station coloured by its state and showing its active step number and name. Mode selector, Start / Stop / Reset. Good, reject, total counts. DB_Production.*, DB_HMI.* 2 Station detail (x3) GRAPH overview control bound to the station's GRAPH instance DB: active step, step time, interlock and supervision status. Text of the current step. GR_StationN instance DB 3 Manual / Setup One row per actuator: jog button, current position feedback, and the interlock condition as a lamp + text ("Blocked: Z not at top"). Visible and enabled only in Manual / Setup. process tags, interlock bits from FB_StationN 4 Alarms Alarm view (active + history), acknowledge button, filter by station. system alarms 5 Production OEE and its three factors since counter reset, cycle time vs ideal, counter reset button (with confirmation). DB_Production.*

docs.title: Operating modes, interlocks and alarms
docs.text: This follows the structure SICAR-style cells use: one mode manager for the cell, one GRAPH sequence per station, and the same interlocks guarding both automatic and manual motion.

docs.title: Modes and cell states
docs.text:
Mode Selected by What runs Allowed transitions Auto HMI or panel selector, cell stopped All GRAPH sequences in automatic, Start / Stop from panel or HMI to Manual or Setup only when stopped Manual HMI, cell stopped GRAPH sequences switched to manual (SW_MAN); actuators jog from the Manual screen, each guarded by its interlock to Auto only after a homing check (all actuators at their home limit) Setup HMI, cell stopped GRAPH in tap mode (SW_TAP): one step per Start press, for commissioning to Auto after homing check

Cell state (published as DB_Production.CellState): Stopped (0), Running (1), Fault (2). A station fault holds the whole cell: every sequence stops advancing until Reset. This is a deliberate simplification; a real line often lets other stations empty out.

E-stop removes the Cell_EStop signal: all outputs drop, all sequences are reset to their initial step (INIT_SQ) after the E-stop is released and Reset is pressed. In Factory I/O this is a functional model only; real safety would be on a fail-safe F-CPU.

docs.title: Stack light
docs.text: Light Meaning Green steady Auto, running Yellow steady Stopped, or Manual / Setup Yellow flashing Fault cleared, waiting for Start Red flashing Active fault, not acknowledged Red steady Fault acknowledged, condition still present

docs.title: Manual-mode interlocks
docs.text:
Each jog button on the HMI is enabled only when its interlock is TRUE, and the HMI shows the interlock state next to the button so the operator sees why a move is blocked.

Actuator Jog Interlock S1_RejectPusher Extend Infeed conveyor stopped S1_ConvInfeed Run Pusher at back S2_PP_Z Down X at pick OR X at place S2_PP_X Move Z at top S2_PP_Grab Release Z at bottom (never drop a lid from the top) S2_StopBlade Lower Clamp open AND Z at top S2_Clamp Open Z at top S3_ConvOutfeed Run none

docs.title: Alarms
docs.text:
Every supervision fault in 02_sequences.md is one alarm, numbered by its fault code (101 to 302). Two ways to raise it in TIA, use the first:

  1. GRAPH supervision + ProDiag / system diagnostics. With the GRAPH FBs set to report supervision errors, TIA creates the alarm with the step text automatically and the WinCC alarm view shows it with no extra code.
  2. Program alarm (Program_Alarm) in FB_Production, triggered from ActiveFaultCode, if the automatic alarms are not available in your license.

Either way FB_Production also writes the fault into DB_Production (code, station, step, start time, duration) for the OPC UA dashboard.

Additional cell-level alarms (not from GRAPH):

Code Text 1 Emergency stop pressed 2 Mode change refused, cell running 3 Homing check failed, cannot enter Auto

docs.title: OPC UA interface
docs.text:
Generated from python/cellsim/tags.py by python/tools/gen_docs.py.

Namespace URI: http://www.siemens.com/simatic-s7-opcua. Node ids are ns=<index of that URI>;s="DB"."Variable", which is how an S7-1500 publishes global DB variables. Resolve the index by URI at connect time; do not hard-code ns=3.

In TIA Portal: CPU properties > OPC UA > Server > Activate, then set the DBs below as Accessible from HMI/OPC UA (and Writable for DB_HMI). DB_Sim exists only in the mock server.

Node (string id) PLC type Access Description "DB_Production"."CellState" Int read 0 Stopped, 1 Running, 2 Fault "DB_Production"."CellMode" Int read 1 Auto, 2 Manual, 3 Setup (mirror of DB_HMI.Mode) "DB_Production"."GoodCount" DInt read Good parts at outfeed since counter reset "DB_Production"."RejectCount" DInt read Parts rejected at inspection "DB_Production"."TotalCount" DInt read GoodCount + RejectCount "DB_Production"."LastCycleTime_ms" DInt read Time between the last two good parts "DB_Production"."IdealCycleTime_ms" DInt read Design cycle time per part "DB_Production"."PlannedTime_s" Real read Time in Auto with the cell started "DB_Production"."RunTime_s" Real read Planned time minus fault downtime "DB_Production"."ActiveFaultCode" Int read 0 when no fault is active "DB_Production"."ActiveFaultStation" Int read Station of the active fault "DB_Production"."ActiveFaultStep" Int read GRAPH step of the active fault "DB_Production"."FaultSeq" DInt read Increments when a fault starts "DB_Production"."FaultClearedSeq" DInt read Increments when a fault is reset "DB_Production"."LastFaultCode" Int read Code of the last cleared fault "DB_Production"."LastFaultStation" Int read Station of the last cleared fault "DB_Production"."LastFaultDuration_s" Real read Downtime of the last cleared fault "DB_Production"."S1_ActiveStep" Int read Active GRAPH step, station 1 "DB_Production"."S2_ActiveStep" Int read Active GRAPH step, station 2 "DB_Production"."S3_ActiveStep" Int read Active GRAPH step, station 3 "DB_HMI"."Mode" Int read/write Requested mode, 1 Auto, 2 Manual, 3 Setup "DB_HMI"."Cmd_Start" Bool read/write Start pulse "DB_HMI"."Cmd_Stop" Bool read/write Stop pulse "DB_HMI"."Cmd_Reset" Bool read/write Fault reset / acknowledge pulse "DB_Sim"."InjectFaultStation" Int read/write Write 1-3 to jam the current step of that station

Enumerations: CellState 0 Stopped, 1 Running, 2 Fault. Mode 1 Auto, 2 Manual, 3 Setup.

Event pattern: the PLC increments FaultClearedSeq after it has written LastFaultCode, LastFaultStation and LastFaultDuration_s. The collector subscribes to the sequence counter and then reads the three detail tags, so a client never sees half-written fault data.

docs.title: S7-GRAPH sequences
docs.text:
Generated from python/cellsim/sequences.py by python/tools/gen_docs.py. Edit the Python file, then regenerate, so the simulator and this spec never drift.

Conventions, matching how the sequences are built in S7-GRAPH:

  • Action = what the step does (N = non-stored action unless stated).
  • Transition = condition to leave the step.
  • Interlock (C) = must stay TRUE for the step's actions to run. If it drops, the actions stop and an interlock error is shown; the step does not advance.
  • Supervision (V) = the step faults if its transition is not met in time: V: S_NO_TIME > T#<limit>. The fault code becomes the alarm number.
  • Wait steps have no supervision: a starved or blocked station is not a fault.
  • Ideal cycle time used for OEE performance: 6.0 s per part.

docs.title: Station 1: Infeed and inspection (GR_Station1)
docs.text:
Step Name Action Transition Interlock (C) Nominal (s) Supervision (V) Fault S1 Wait for part Infeed conveyor ON S1_PartAtEntry Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault wait - - S2 Convey to vision Infeed conveyor ON S1_PartAtVision Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault 1.5 4 s 101 Part did not reach the vision sensor S3 Read part type Infeed conveyor OFF, latch S1_VisionType S1_VisionType <> 0 Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault 0.3 1 s 102 Vision sensor read timeout S4 Extend reject pusher S1_RejectPusher ON S1_PusherFront Infeed conveyor OFF AND S1_PusherBack was TRUE 0.6 2 s 103 Reject pusher did not reach front position S5 Retract reject pusher S1_RejectPusher OFF S1_PusherBack Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault 0.6 2 s 104 Reject pusher did not return to back position S6 Wait for station 2 ready - S2_ReadyForPart Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault wait - - S7 Transfer to station 2 Infeed and transfer conveyors ON S2_BaseAtStop S2_StopBlade UP AND S1_PusherBack 1.2 4 s 105 Part transfer to station 2 timed out

Branch after S3: wrong part type goes S4 -> S5 -> S1 (reject, RejectCount + 1); right part goes S6 -> S7 -> S1.

docs.text:
Step Name Action Transition Interlock (C) Nominal (s) Supervision (V) Fault S1 Wait for part - S3_PartAtEntry Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault wait - - S2 Convey to counter Outfeed conveyor ON S3_PartCount Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault 1.5 4 s 301 Part not seen at outfeed counter S3 Count and remove Increment GoodCount, outfeed ON S3_PartAtExit falling edge Mode=Auto AND NOT Cell_Fault 0.4 1 s 302 Part did not clear the outfeed

S3 -> S1 and GoodCount + 1 on the falling edge of S3_PartAtExit.

docs.title: Handshakes between sequences
docs.text:
Signal Set by Reset by Meaning S2_ReadyForPart GR_Station2 in S1 GR_Station2 leaving S2 Station 2 can accept a base S3_ReadyForPart GR_Station3 in S1 GR_Station3 leaving S2 Station 3 can accept a part

Each sequence only reads the other's ready bit; no output is written by two sequences.

docs.title: Collector, data model and dashboard
docs.text:
PLC or mock ──OPC UA──► collector.py ──► data/cell.db (SQLite) ──► app.py (Streamlit, read-only)

The dashboard never connects to the PLC. Only the collector does, and it only reads, so the dashboard cannot change anything on the cell.

docs.title: Collector (python/dashboard/collector.py)
docs.text:
python -m dashboard.collector --url opc.tcp://localhost:4840 --db data/cell.db --period 1.0
  • Resolves the namespace index from the Siemens URI http://www.siemens.com/simatic-s7-opcua at connect time, so the same code works on the mock and on PLCSIM Advanced.
  • Subscription (100 ms publishing interval, queue 50) on FaultClearedSeq and TotalCount:
  • FaultClearedSeq changed → read LastFaultCode, LastFaultStation, LastFaultDuration_s → one row in faults. A jump of more than 1 is logged as missed records.
  • TotalCount rose → read LastCycleTime_ms → one row in cycles.
  • Polling every --period seconds → one row in snapshots with all counters and states.

docs.title: SQLite schema
docs.text:
Table Columns One row per snapshots ts, planned_s, run_s, total, good, reject, ideal_ms, cell_state, mode, active_fault_code, active_fault_station, active_fault_step, s1_step, s2_step, s3_step poll period cycles ts, total, cycle_ms part counted faults ts, seq (unique), code, station, text, duration_s fault cleared

ts is wall-clock Unix time on the collector PC. Durations (planned_s, run_s, cycle_ms, duration_s) are PLC time, so they stay correct when the mock runs faster than real time.

docs.title: KPIs (python/dashboard/oee.py)
docs.text:
OEE = A × P × Q
A = RunTime / PlannedTime
P = IdealCycleTime × TotalCount / RunTime
Q = GoodCount / TotalCount
  • Rolling OEE over N planned minutes uses counter deltas between the newest snapshot and the last snapshot at least N minutes of planned time earlier. Idle time outside Auto does not dilute the window.
  • OEE since reset uses the absolute counters.
  • Pareto: downtime summed per fault code, largest first, with cumulative share.
  • MTBF per station = cell run time / faults at that station. MTTR = mean fault duration.
  • Ideal cycle time is 6.0 s per part, set in sequences.py and published as IdealCycleTime_ms.

docs.title: Dashboard (python/dashboard/app.py)
docs.text:
streamlit run dashboard/app.py -- --db ../data/cell.db

Refreshes every 2 s. Contents, top to bottom:

  1. Status banner: running, stopped, or the active fault with code, station, step and text.
  2. KPI tiles: rolling OEE and its three factors, OEE since reset, good / reject counts.
  3. Rolling OEE trend with an 85 % benchmark line, and cycle time per good part against the ideal.
  4. Downtime Pareto by fault, MTBF / MTTR per station, and the active GRAPH step of each station.
  5. Fault history table, newest first.

The OEE window (5 to 120 planned minutes) is set in the sidebar.

docs.title: Sample run
docs.text:
Mock at 30× speed, fault probability doubled to 0.004 so a short run shows enough faults, two injected faults, about 45 minutes of PLC time:

Metric Value OEE (last 30 min) 66.0 % Availability / Performance / Quality 72.5 % / 98.0 % / 93.0 % Good / reject 257 / 19 Mean cycle time about 6.5 s (ideal 6.0 s) Top downtime fault 301 Part not seen at outfeed counter Most faults Station 2 (9 faults, MTBF 3.2 min, MTTR 38 s)

With the default fault probability, OEE settles above 80 %.

docs.title: Mock PLC and cell simulator
docs.text:
python/cellsim stands in for the S7-1500 until the TIA Portal project exists. It has two layers:

Module Role sequences.py The three station sequences as data: steps, actions, transitions, interlocks, nominal times, supervision limits, fault codes and texts. Single source of truth for the simulator, docs/02_sequences.md and the dashboard's fault texts. tags.py The OPC UA tag contract: DB, name, PLC type, access, description. Shared by the server, the collector and docs/05_opcua_interface.md. model.py Time-stepped model of the cell (pure Python, no I/O, deterministic for a seed). server.py asyncua OPC UA server that runs the model and publishes the tags. cmd.py Command-line HMI: start, stop, reset, mode, fault injection.

docs.title: How the model works
docs.text:
Every tick (default 0.1 s of PLC time) the model advances all three station sequences side by side.

  • Timed steps last their nominal time with ±10 % jitter. Each has a supervision limit; if a step is jammed it never completes and faults once the limit is reached, exactly like S7-GRAPH supervision (V).
  • Wait steps (starved or blocked) wait on a handshake and are never supervised.
  • Handshakes are two one-part buffers: station 1 → 2 and station 2 → 3. A station only hands a part on when the next buffer is empty.
  • Inspection: after reading the part type, station 1 rejects a share of parts (--reject-rate, default 5 %) through the pusher branch.
  • Faults: any timed step can jam at random (--fault-prob, default 0.2 % per step execution), or on demand with cmd inject <station>. A fault holds the whole cell until reset.
  • Reset: by default a simulated operator resets after a random repair time (exponential, mean 45 s, minimum 5 s). With --manual-reset faults wait for cmd reset. After reset the faulted step restarts, like GRAPH ACK_EF.
  • Time accounting matches FB_Production: PlannedTime counts in Auto while started (faults included), RunTime counts only when no fault is active.

docs.title: Server options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning --endpoint opc.tcp://0.0.0.0:4840 OPC UA endpoint --speed 10 Simulation speed vs wall clock --seed 1 Random seed (same seed, same run) --fault-prob 0.002 Jam chance per timed step --reject-rate 0.05 Share of parts rejected at inspection --manual-reset off Faults wait for cmd reset --stopped off Start with the cell stopped (send cmd start)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
python -m cellsim.cmd start | stop | reset
python -m cellsim.cmd mode 2        # 1 Auto, 2 Manual, 3 Setup (refused while running)
python -m cellsim.cmd inject 2      # jam the current timed step of station 2

cmd start/stop/reset/mode also work against the real PLC, because they write DB_HMI; inject exists only in the mock (DB_Sim).

docs.title: Known simplifications
docs.text:
• One fault holds the whole cell; a real line often lets other stations empty out.
  • Sensors are not modelled individually; a step is either on time, jittered, or jammed.
  • No Manual-mode motion: in Manual the model just stops counting planned time.
  • Right after a fault on station 3, a part already waiting at station 2 can give one short cycle-time reading (about 2.4 s). A real PLC measuring time between good parts would record the same.
